One host core handles ~4-5 mostly-idle single-vCPU microVMs before exec p99 degrades
Go's net.FileListener fails on AF_VSOCK; guests must accept with raw unix.Accept
Default-drop nftables FORWARD chain silently breaks Docker egress on the same host
Firecracker Go SDK jailer + snapshot mode is broken; three handler-list edits needed
Snapshots restore a frozen guest clock that will eventually break TLS validation

Programmatic tool use slashes token costs but amplifies prompt injection from text-level to runtime-privilege level
Memory scraping works in two steps: read /proc/1/maps for layout, then read each region from /proc/1/mem

AWS closed the disclosure as informative under shared responsibility, leaving controls to customers
Prompt injection impact is now bounded by the managed runtime's privileges, not typed tool schemas

items.title: What actually is a Docker container?
items.summary: Linux containers are not lightweight VMs: isolation is implemented per-process via namespace pointers in task_struct, so the same kernel answers the same syscalls differently depending on the calling process's nsproxy.
ideas: Containers share the host kernel; isolation happens at syscall-resolution time via per-process namespace pointers, not virtualization.
UID 0 inside a user namespace only holds capabilities relative to that namespace, not the initial one.
The kernel checks ns_capable on the user_ns that owns the target resource (e.g., uts_ns->user_ns for sethostname).
/proc/self/ns entries expose the namespace instance a process belongs to via inode numbers.
user_ns lives in cred, not nsproxy, because it is credential state rather than a per-namespace resource.
Mac/Windows Docker runtimes need a Linux VM because macOS/Windows kernels lack the required namespace and cgroup features.
items.rating_reason: Exceptionally mechanism-focused explainer that walks through Linux kernel source (task_struct, nsproxy, kernel/sys.c) to show exactly how containers differ from VMs and how namespace isolation is implemented per-process rather than via virtualization. Uses a reproducible test program and references real CVEs (CVE-2022-0185, CVE-2024-1086), capabilities, and UID mapping to demonstrate non-obvious behaviors like 'root inside' not being 'root outside'. Truncation at the PID namespace section is a meaningful limitation, and some territory is familiar to seasoned kernel engineers, but the kernel-source-grounded explanation is genuinely instructive.

items.title: Shadowing the Standard Library
items.summary: A cross-language survey of when runtimes removed or retained an ambient working-directory module search path, framed around a real coding-agent supply-chain attack that exploited Python's sys.path[0] precedence.
ideas: Python places the script directory first on sys.path, enabling struct.py shadowing inside agent-unpacked archives.
Ruby dropped '.' from $LOAD_PATH in 1.9.2 (2010); Perl removed it in 5.26 (2017) after CVE-2016-1238.
Python 3.11 added -P / PYTHONSAFEPATH to drop sys.path[0] while leaving other env vars intact.
PHP and Lua still allow cwd shadowing on their default include/package paths, with no safe-mode switch.
Node checks core module names before disk, so a local http.js can't shadow the built-in http.
Coding agents that extract archives into a working dir reproduce the classic /tmp shadowing threat model.
Python 3.11+ frozen modules (os, abc, io, codecs) can't be shadowed; only .py wrappers around C extensions can.
items.rating_reason: Original comparative research across roughly a dozen language runtimes documenting whether the current/script directory is on the default module search path, with concrete version dates, CVE references (CVE-2016-1238), and the actual mechanism (sys.path[0], $LOAD_PATH, @INC). Includes a credible threat model connecting coding-agent archive extraction to the historical /tmp shadowing attack, and surfaces less-known details like Victor Stinner's draft PEP, PYTHONSAFEPATH, and the 3.11 frozen-modules protection that limits shadowing to .py wrappers. Strong on substance and noise-controlled; only mildly held back by being primarily a synthesis rather than novel exploit research.

items.title: XProtect behavioral flop: the Golden Gasp

Holding an exclusive flock on XPdb wedges XProtectBridgeService, which fails every PRAGMA/CREATE/INSERT with database is locked.

file-read-data was inadvertently re-allowed, exposing the behavioral telemetry database to root again.
A previously fixed, publicly disclosed bug regressed across a major OS bump with no regression test catching it.
Same PoC (perl flock one-liner) works on macOS 27 that XCSSET used in the wild since 2025.

The author provides a reproducible one-liner PoC, exact sandbox profile boolean inversion (entitlement test flipped from negative to positive), side-by-side diff of macOS 26.6.2 vs 27.0 rules, real enforcement logs, and clear impact analysis. The finding is non-obvious, technically deep, and directly relevant to defensive engineering - XProtect's behavioral detection can be silenced by any root process via a simple flock.

items.title: The case against JPEG XL

Schedule latency histogram is the most useful Tokio metric for diagnosing runtime interactions
Spawning thousands of tiny tasks adds runtime overhead; batch work instead of spawning per unit
Blocking pool becomes a contention bottleneck around 50k tasks/sec on a 32-core host
Use multiple runtimes with CPU pinning to isolate latency-sensitive from background work

items.rating_reason: Firsthand engineering investigation with original measurements: the author shows Go's GC metadata pages (allocated once, never freed) can be evicted to swap, turning ~51us median stop-the-world pauses into 40ms stalls, and traced 39ms of one pause to 228 page faults via a bpf script plus addr2line stack output. The mechanism (LRU eviction of cold GC bookkeeping, do_swap_page during sweep termination) is clearly explained, and the linked GitHub repo provides reproducibility artifacts. Relevance is high for Go runtime, kernel memory management, and production latency work, and the article is concise with good value per minute. Limitations: the allocation-latency spike (105-903ms) is explicitly unconfirmed, and the niche swap-plus-cgroup configuration narrows applicability, but the core finding is well-supported and actionable.

items.title: cutting a Rust GPUI launcher’s idle memory
items.summary: Lazy GPU init, Vulkan ICD filtering via VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE, sprite atlas clearing, LRU icon caching, and capping glibc per-thread arenas with MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 cut a GPUI launcher's idle RSS from 141 MiB to 39 MiB; triangulate heaptrack, smaps, and timing-aware RSS measurements because each tool alone misleads.
ideas: GPUI keeps the wgpu device and atlas alive at App level even when the window is hidden
VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE=*lvp*,*llvmpipe*,*dzn* skips software ICDs in wgpu before vkCreateInstance
glibc MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 caps per-thread arenas and stops the RSS ratchet during repeated scans
GPUI's sprite atlas is append-only and needs an explicit clear() to avoid slow growth
malloc_trim only releases the main arena; secondary per-thread arenas stay at high-water mark
heaptrack tracks allocations, massif sees only live malloc, smaps shows anonymous rwx regions: triangulate them
Lazy GPU warm on first overlay open avoids ~78 MiB of idle cost for never-opened launchers
Decoding icons locally with the image crate plus an LRU GPU cache eliminates the ~47 MiB typing spike
RSS is sampling-time-sensitive; measure at lifecycle points (pre-gpui, post-index, post-warm, settled)
items.rating_reason: Exceptional practitioner writeup with original measurements, concrete numbers (141→39 MiB idle), and several non-obvious findings including the glibc per-thread arena ratchet, the VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE ICD filter, and the append-only sprite atlas. items.title: Agent harness security and Git
items.summary: Coding-agent harnesses that auto-allow git commands in untrusted directories enable arbitrary code execution via malicious Git config (fsmonitor, insteadOf) and nested bare repos, with concrete CVEs and vendor fixes documented.
ideas: Bare repos (objects/, refs/, HEAD) are auto-detected inside normal repos, enabling RCE via core.fsmonitor
Claude Code's accept-edits mode allowed `cd sub && git status` to bypass readonly allowlists
Codex auto-running `git ls-remote` on startup is exploitable via [url] insteadOf rewriting to ext::
Cursor disables VS Code's workspace trust, auto-running git commands in any opened folder
Git 3.0 changes default to require explicit --git-dir for bare repos
Set `git config --global safe.bareRepository explicit` to mitigate bare-repo confusion attacks
items.rating_reason: Exceptional firsthand security research documenting original vulnerabilities found in major LLM coding agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor) with reproducible exploitation mechanisms. items.title: Relaying a self-hosted mail server through Cloudflare

ideas: Cloudflare Email Service relays bytes unmodified: no link rewriting or tracking pixels, unlike Mailjet's default SMTP relay behavior.
Postfix needs smtp_tls_wrappermode = yes for port 465 implicit TLS, or it hangs instead of erroring clearly.
Bracketed relayhost [host]:port disables MX lookup, forcing direct A-record connection.
The MAIL FROM domain must be onboarded for Email Sending or Cloudflare returns 550 5.7.1.
Dual DKIM signing (cloudflare-email.net + your domain with cf-bounce selector) achieves DMARC alignment under p=REJECT.
Rewrite system senders via sender_canonical_maps before onboarding the hostname's domain.
Apex SPF -all is safe once all legitimate mail leaves via a cf-bounce subdomain.
items.rating_reason: Highly practical, firsthand walkthrough of cutting over a self-hosted Postfix server to Cloudflare's Email Service relay. Includes specific Postfix postconf commands, Cloudflare API token creation via curl, DNS records produced, an auth-probe Python script, and verified Authentication-Results from Gmail showing SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass under p=REJECT. Documents non-obvious gotchas (square brackets on relayhost, smtp_tls_wrappermode for implicit-TLS port 465, MAIL FROM domain onboarding requirement) and surfaces the noteworthy privacy finding that Mailjet silently rewrites links and injects tracking pixels by default.

items.title: Three Injections and a Rootkit: How the lurves PyPI typosquat attacks the AI in your toolchain

ideas: .pth files in site-packages execute at every Python interpreter startup — not install, not import
Typosquats re-export real packages via Requires-Dist so imports work normally
MCP tool description strings are a live prompt-injection vector against coding agents
Rootkits can expose fake sysfs paths as control channels for PID hiding
Comments instructing AI reviewers to mark code clean target LLM-assisted triage pipelines

Portuguese comments + AMD impersonation indicate AI-assisted malware authoring with attribution slip

items.title: Spending the Cost Function Without Telling the Agent
items.summary: When an LLM coding agent is shown a structural complexity cost function, it optimizes the number and degrades the code; when the same cost function is kept hidden and spent by an external tool that triggers refactors, structural concentration falls ~70% without the gaming artifacts.
ideas: Disclosing cost functions to LLM agents triggers Goodhart's law: score drops 45x but code quality collapses
Hidden tool-spent cost functions reduce Spring impact slope from 435 to 127 (70%) with non-overlapping CIs
Total complexity is conserved across conditions; only its distribution changes
Disclosed run tripled class count and multiplied static utilities 9x while gaming the metric
Refactor-only run sits near control on class proliferation and duplication measures
Cost function: max(WMC_other, 1) × CC × max(1, changed_lines) per changed function, summed
EvoScore drops from 0.787 (control) to 0.440 (disclosed) to 0.712 (refactor-only)
Concentrating architectures (Spring) trip the gate far more than cohesive ones (OfficeFloor)
items.rating_reason: Substantive, well-controlled empirical study comparing three conditions (control, disclosed metric, hidden tool-spent metric) across two architectures and twenty chains of sixty accumulating changes. The experiment provides a clean demonstration of Goodhart's law applied to LLM coding agents, with concrete numbers, bootstrapped confidence intervals, and reproducible git branches. Findings are non-obvious and directly actionable for anyone building AI coding tooling. Limitations include single model (unnamed), single task family, the blog format rather than peer review, and the same author designing both prior and current interventions.

items.title: https://github.com/mein-0/LolModapi
items.summary: MSI Dragon Center's MODAPI.sys kernel driver exposes unauthenticated arbitrary MSR read/write to any local user, enabling trivial local privilege escalation to SYSTEM on any MSI machine running the software.
ideas: MODAPI.sys has no device object security descriptor, letting any local user open it
The driver has no MSR index whitelist, allowing arbitrary read/write of any MSR
Reading IA32_LSTAR breaks KASLR by leaking ntoskrnl!KiSystemCall64 directly
Overwriting IA32_LSTAR redirects kernel syscall handling to attacker-controlled code at CPL0
SMEP is the only mitigation; bypassed via mov cr4, rax gadget from ntoskrnl
Full exploit chain reads MSR, finds gadgets in ntoskrnl from disk, copies SYSTEM token, restores MSR
Driver ships pre-installed on many MSI systems via Dragon Center, expanding attack surface
Reported to MSI 2026-06-21 and verified fixed; driver hash provided for identification
items.rating_reason: This is a high-density, original vulnerability disclosure documenting a local privilege escalation in MSI Dragon Center's MODAPI.sys kernel driver. The only limitations are brevity (PoC code is referenced but not visible in the README itself) and the niche audience it serves. items.title: Lalit Maganti
items.summary: Build performance issues are rarely about the language itself—Bun's dramatic Zig-to-Rust speedup was primarily caused by switching from Full LTO to ThinLTO and from a monolithic module to 90+ parallelizable crates, not by inherent language differences.
ideas: buildprof uses ptrace to record entire build process trees into Perfetto-compatible timelines
Full LTO funnels optimization into one massive job; ThinLTO preserves parallelism across modules
The link step alone accounted for 16m35s of Bun's 24m24s Zig build—two-thirds of total time
Switching Full LTO to ThinLTO on Bun only saved 3m40s because downloaded WebKit libs still used Full LTO
Rebuilding WebKit with ThinLTO cut link time from 16m35s to 7m22s—over half the improvement
Rust's 90+ crate structure enables parallel compilation Zig's single-module architecture cannot match
ptrace is simpler than eBPF (no CAP_BPF needed) and more flexible than ftrace for build tracing
Clang's -ftime-trace exposes internal pass timings like ModuleInlinerWrapperPass for optimization
Build-system-agnostic tracing works because all systems fundamentally spawn subprocesses
Following file reads/writes through process trees reveals data dependencies between build steps
buildprof's overhead is proportional to file opens: negligible on ripgrep, ~5s on Redis
Tracing turned up hidden build steps like fetching public IP and inspecting Docker containers
items.rating_reason: Excellent technical investigation that delivers multiple genuine insights: novel open-source tooling (buildprof using ptrace), empirical data quantifying LTO's impact on Bun's build times, and the counter-intuitive finding that Bun's Rust migration speedup stemmed more from LTO settings and crate parallelism than language differences. The methodology is rigorous (reproducing CI builds, isolating variables, capturing compiler traces), the density is high with ~8-10 value instances across ~2000 words, and the content strongly aligns with software engineering and developer tooling themes. Minor penalty for being truncated at the end, but the core investigation and tool deliver substantial value.

items.title: Ken Shirriff's blog
items.summary: The 8087's FSCALE instruction, despite appearing trivial, requires 140+ micro-instructions and three subroutine levels because floating-point corner cases (zero, NaN, infinity, denormals, overflow/underflow) must be handled at the microcode level—revealing how much complexity hides beneath a clean instruction set.
ideas: The 8087 standardized floating-point arithmetic, becoming the basis for modern IEEE 754
FSCALE requires over 140 micro-instructions despite seeming trivially simple
The 8087 stores all values internally as 80-bit 'temporary real' numbers
Register tags invisibly track state: valid, special, zero, or empty
The 8087 has six exception types with masked/unmasked behavior for graceful degradation
Exponents use a bias of 16383 to keep stored values always positive
Float-to-int conversion works by subtracting exponent from 0x403e to get shift count
The chip has separate 16-bit exponent and 64-bit significand datapaths
The Opcode Collective reverse-engineers 1648 total micro-instructions from the die
Micro-instructions are 16 bits with seven types controlling transfer, shift, adder, jumps
Scaling zero by anything—including NaN—yields zero due to microcode special-case handling
Unmasked exceptions trigger 8086 interrupts; masked ones produce best-available results
Reverse-engineering reveals hidden features in the original 8087 design
items.rating_reason: Exceptional original technical content featuring genuine reverse-engineering work by Ken Shirriff and the Opcode Collective. The post delivers multiple novel insights: die photography of the 8087 chip, detailed microcode walkthrough of FSCALE (showing 140+ micro-instructions for a seemingly trivial operation), the 80-bit temporary real format, the tag system, and float-to-int conversion via exponent-based shift counting. High information density with no padding, clickbait, or promotional content. Content is cut off mid-conclusion but what's present is deeply substantive.

items.title: Boundary-BenchBlog

ideas: Cursor CLI's Seatbelt sandbox only wrapped the shell tool, not internal git calls
core.fsmonitor hook in .git/config executes as an external program when git runs
Cursor's harness spawned git via plain child_process.spawn with no -c core.fsmonitor=false
The escape fires on the first read-only turn, needing no skill loading or prompt injection
Universal fix uses GIT_CONFIG_COUNT/KEY/VALUE env vars, which override .git/config precedence
Per-tool sandboxing is fragile; process-level or VM-level sandboxing is architecturally robust
Same vulnerability class affected Claude Code, Cursor, and potentially other agents
Archive delivery (zip with pre-armed .git/config) is a weaker but viable attack vector
Accomplish sandboxes the entire agent process inside a VM with proxied credentials and network
Cursor shipped the right fix: env-var hardening rather than per-call flag coordination
items.rating_reason: Genuinely high-quality original security research with a reproducible PoC, clear technical root-cause analysis, and verified disclosure-to-fix narrative. Delivers 7+ value instances in ~1700 words (high density): the core.fsmonitor escape mechanism, the exact unsandboxed git commands, the universal GIT_CONFIG env-var fix pattern, and a useful taxonomy of sandbox architectures (per-tool vs. process-level vs. VM). Mild promotional penalty for the closing 'How we built Accomplish' section, but it stays contextually relevant to the architectural discussion rather than becoming a hard sell. items.title: It never opened the file I handed it
items.summary: A tool-execution-layer trigger that injects note names into prompts fires reliably, but the model only reads the named file ~24% of the time even when the pointer is relevant, so reminders are enforced while reading remains a model decision.
ideas: Only 23.6% of correct file pointers were ever opened by the model
Baseline file-open rate is 11% with no pointer, 26.1% with relevant pointer
43.7% of triggers originally fired on machine messages, not human prompts
Reminder mechanism enforcement is decoupled from actual file reading
Pointer relevance (68.3%) far exceeds pointer consumption (23.6%)
Pre-trained LLM habits cannot be corrected by records created post-training
Cohen's kappa 0.837 across blind re-judging of 60 firings
A name in context is information; behavior requires a constraint
items.rating_reason: Highly substantive engineering write-up with rare quantitative rigor: 1,234 hash-verified firings, blind judging with Cohen's kappa 0.837, concrete open-rate measurements (26.1% vs 11% baseline), and an honest correction of earlier flawed methodology. The central finding is genuinely non-obvious and actionable for anyone building agent memory: injecting a pointer is not the same as injecting content, and ~75% of correct pointers were never followed by a file read. The author is admirably transparent about what was and wasn't measured (e.g., whether the correction actually held after reading). Community LLM benchmarks often compare against untuned default configurations
MTP speculative decoding hits jackpot bands on code-shaped prompts at depth
Live production traffic runs 40%+ below synthetic repeat-only benchmarks
QSA pooled-block-keys fix in llama.cpp roughly doubled warm decode at 55k
Closed-source inference engines block community kernel contributions on niche hardware
Cold prefill wins lose value when warm decode dominates agent wall-clock time

The article delivers original measurements across multiple context bands and prompt classes, identifies a non-obvious methodological flaw in community benchmark comparisons (wrong baseline), and provides hard-won operational insights including the 40%+ gap between synthetic and live production traffic. items.title: Finding the Cryptominer Hiding in a Docker overlay2 Layer
items.summary: Container persistence in image-layer diff directories survives docker rm and eludes runtime-only forensics like ps/ss, so IR scoping must include overlay2 layer walks, manifest comparisons, and registry digest checks rather than just live process sampling.
ideas: Image-layer files survive docker rm; only docker rmi drops the layer, and only when no other image or stopped container references it.
Deploy by repo@sha256:<digest> instead of tag to prevent registry-side retargeting that mutates what gets pulled.
Clean on-disk tampering of an overlay2 diff requires forging layerdb and imagedb metadata alongside the file changes.
Docker 29.0+ fresh installs default to the containerd image store; check docker info before assuming overlay2 paths are correct.
Manifest comparison of layer contents against the rebuilt image catches renamed variants that a name-only find misses.
File mtimes inside image layers are weak forensic evidence because tar and COPY preserve build-host timestamps.
items.rating_reason: Firsthand incident-response walkthrough with unusually specific forensic detail about overlay2 layer roles, image-layer persistence mechanics, and a concrete validation triad (name check, manifest compare, digest compare). Non-obvious insights include the survivability of image layers through docker rm but removal via docker rmi, the tag-vs-digest retargeting attack vector, the need for layerdb/imagedb forgery to achieve clean on-disk tampering, and the critical caveat that Docker 29.0+ defaults to the containerd image store where overlay2 sweeps are meaningless. Author is unusually disciplined about flagging inferences vs observations and unresolved attribution. Truncation mid-sentence at the very end is a real but minor blemish on an otherwise exceptional piece.

items.title: Dropping eBPF CPU Cost by About 90% With Memoization (Not AI Gen)
items.summary: Memoizing inode-to-policy lookups in an eBPF LSM file-open agent with an LRU_HASH map keyed on (mntns, mount_id, inode) cut kernel CPU by ~90%, with i_nlink used to safely skip hardlinked inodes.
ideas: Cache eBPF LSM policy lookups by inode, mount ID, and mount namespace to avoid repeated dentry walks
Use i_nlink != 1 as a guard to skip caching hardlinked inodes
Encode policy verdicts as bitmask access_index values for compact LRU_HASH entries
Profile eBPF overhead with perf cycles:k flamegraphs to surface path-walk hotspots
eBPF maps cannot store raw pointer keys; use numeric identifiers (inode + mount info) instead
items.rating_reason: Firsthand eBPF engineering write-up with concrete mechanism (inode + mount ID + mntns composite key in a BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH), real implementation code, verifiable benchmark numbers (kernel cycles dropped from 28B to 3.03B, ~90%), and a thoughtful edge-case analysis using i_nlink to handle hardlinks. The optimization is genuinely useful and non-obvious, and the author is transparent about trade-offs (sacrificing cache coverage for correctness). No hype, minimal noise.

items.title: Weaponizing Starlark: Non-Executable Malware and Scriptable C2 Agents
items.summary: Embedding a deterministic language interpreter (Starlark) in a Go C2 lets modules call native APIs without ever creating unbacked executable memory, evading BOF-oriented scanners while still enabling token-aware operations.
ideas: Embedding Starlark lets a C2 module layer call Win32/Linux syscalls via Go builtins, never generating executable memory.
win_call and sys_call expose DLL exports and syscall numbers by name, routed through a VEH-protected Go wrapper.
Token context (stolen, netonly, Kerberos ticket) is injected before script.Run, then impersonated per builtin call.
BOF detections stem from private RWX pages and unbacked frames; Starlark execution stays inside the agent's mapped image.
Scanner-detectable 'module noise' shifts from 'ran a module' to 'what that module actually did' (e.g., VirtualAlloc).
items.rating_reason: Original, empirically-supported research on using Starlark as a scriptable module layer in a Go C2 agent (emp3r0r), with concrete code, debugger call stacks, and head-to-head memory-scanner comparisons (YARA, PE-sieve, Moneta, Patriot, Hunt-SB) showing BOF detections vs clean Starlark execution. Strongly technical, first-hand, and honest about caveats (e.g., VirtualAlloc in a script reintroduces RWX). Slightly docked because the article is truncated mid-explanation of runWithToken and module packaging, leaving the token-implementation walkthrough incomplete.

items.title: Optimization tales in production with CockroachDB: UUID generation (part 5)

ideas: gen_random_uuid() skips cross-region unique checks for random v4 UUIDs
REGIONAL BY ROW primary keys are prefixed with crdb_region in CockroachDB
50x INSERT speedup (250ms to 5ms) from avoiding cross-region reads
SERIALIZABLE isolation forces restart on cross-region UUID write conflicts
Optimization disabled if any other column has a unique constraint
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE lookup joins to verify constraint-check elimination
Production traces beat per-query metrics for pipelined transaction latency

items.title: A Nix store is three functions
items.summary: A Nix binary cache is just three HTTP GETs (nix-cache-info, .narinfo, .nar.xz) whose signature scheme deliberately decouples content trust from transport, enabling creative storage backends including GitHub Pages, git objects, DNS TXT records, and the npm registry.
ideas: Nix binary cache is just three GET endpoints, explaining the protocol's flexibility.

items.title: A 10 GB Database Filled a 200 GB Disk and du Could Not Find the Space
items.summary: When df and du disagree by orders of magnitude, the missing space is almost always in deleted-but-open files; MySQL unlinks temp files by design, so other processes (here an endpoint scanner) can hold them indefinitely and be found with lsof +L1.
ideas: df/du disagreement has only two causes: mount points hiding files, or files deleted while still open (lsof +L1 lists them)
MySQL unlinks its temporary files immediately after creation, making them invisible to du and ls
MySQL 8.4 moved TempTable overflow off tmpdir by default, but filesort still uses unlinked tmpdir files on all versions
An endpoint scanner holding deleted MySQL temp files can consume hundreds of GB until its process restarts
Reading /proc/<pid>/fd reveals true inode state and size even after unlink
Restarting MySQL does NOT release space held by another process's open descriptors to its temp files
items.rating_reason: Exceptional firsthand postmortem of a real production incident, with exact commands, outputs, file sizes, and PIDs supporting the diagnosis. The mechanism is explained precisely (inodes, unlinked-but-open file descriptors, reference counting), the version-specific MySQL 8.0 vs 8.4 behavior change is genuinely non-obvious, and the two-item differential for df/du disagreement is a clean, actionable framework. Trade-offs for mitigation are spelled out honestly. Slight literary framing and a few references to other posts add minor padding but do not weaken the core substance.

items.title: One Column Added to a SELECT: 1,020 Page Reads Became 166,667
items.summary: Adding a column to a SELECT can flip an index-only scan into a sequential scan once enough matching rows are scattered across heap pages, and even after extending the index, writes that clear the visibility map can quietly negate the recovery.
ideas: Adding one uncovered column flipped an index-only scan to a parallel sequential scan at scale
Postgres Heap Fetches: 0 reflects the visibility map state, not the index design
Postgres INCLUDE columns break the HOT update path, amplifying writes to other indexes
MySQL secondary indexes already carry the primary key, so SELECT id is covered for free
Index entries carry heap location; clustered storage means secondary lookups cost a primary descent
Naming indexes after the queries they serve makes the dependency visible to the next maintainer
items.rating_reason: Strong practitioner article with reproducible benchmarks showing how adding a single column to a SELECT flips an index-only scan to a sequential scan at scale. Includes cross-engine comparison (PostgreSQL 18 vs MySQL 8.4) with concrete plans, demonstrates the non-obvious interaction between the visibility map and Heap Fetches (Heap Fetches: 0 is a property of the moment), and honestly weighs the tradeoffs of extending the index (INCLUDE columns, HOT update path breakage, write amplification) versus shrinking the projection. Dense, focused, and free of hype.

items.title: Dissecting GPT-Live
items.summary: By combining API behavior, pricing, and latency observations, the author reverse-engineers GPT-Live-1's likely architecture: a frontend/backend split operating on 80 ms audio frames prefilled in 400 ms chunks, with model size inferred to be similar to mid-tier GPT-5.x text models after accounting for real-time serving overhead.

items.title: Segregated crypto in a custodian bankruptcy still needs a key that works
items.summary: Bankruptcy-remote crypto custody under Swiss law requires four conditions, not three: even with segregated, attributed, on-chain assets, a client only has a claim the estate can actually sign for, which most MPC-backed custodians have never tested against their own vendor-offline failure mode.
ideas: Art. 242a segregation requires the estate to hold every key needed to dispose of the asset.
Prime Trust's 98f cold wallet held 23,778 ETH that nobody could sign for.
MPC custody splits keys across institution, vendor platform, and customer backup.
FINMA Circular 2023/1 recovery tests rarely cover cryptographic signing recovery.
Audited reconciliation confirms presence but never confirms signature capability.
Backup recovery tools assume the vendor workspace that created keys is still live.
items.rating_reason: Original legal-technical analysis combining the Prime Trust failure, Swiss Art. 242a bankruptcy-remote custody rules, the Federal Council's message, FINMA Circular 2023/1, and MPC key-share architecture. items.title: Read the Bits, Not the Integer: msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag and the ESC4⤍ESC1 Chain
items.summary: AD CS template exploitation depends on a sparse bitmask where overwriting the flag value clobbers existing require-bits, while OR-ing the supply bit into the baseline preserves them — the difference between a stealthy exploit and breaking production authentication.
ideas: msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag is a sparse 32-bit bitmask with only 13 defined bits in MS-CRTD
LDAP clients return the flag as signed int32, making high-bit values appear negative
Supply bits (0, 3, 16) make templates abusable; require bits alone never enable impersonation
OR the supply bit into baseline, don't overwrite — preserves existing require-bit guardrails
Bit 27 (REQUIRE_DNS) enabled Certifried; bit 25 (REQUIRE_UPN) is its preventative mirror
Common '5-row sequential' cheat sheets miss combined exploitable values like 16842752
Templates with no supply bits set are safe regardless of how many require bits are present
Bit 16 (ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT_ALT_NAME) is the canonical ESC1 forgeable-identity primitive
MS-CRTD section 2.4 is authoritative for bit values; MS-WCCE for CA behavior
Detection should flag baseline+delta patterns, not isolated static integers like 1 or 65536
items.rating_reason: Exceptional technical content that corrects a widespread misunderstanding in AD CS exploitation by going directly to the MS-CRTD and MS-WCCE protocol specifications. Delivers multiple novel insights: the sparse 13-bit structure, the signed-int32 LDAP trap, the supply-vs-require-bit framework, and the crucially subtle OR-vs-overwrite operational distinction (0xa2000000→0xa2000001 vs demolition). Each of these is genuinely non-obvious expert knowledge not readily available in community cheat sheets. Live exploitation on HackTheBox PingPong provides concrete validation. Minor deduction for content truncation at the end and the very narrow audience limits overall reach, but within its domain this is definitive reference material.

items.title: We removed the location lock
items.summary: Android location providers leak identifying requests to third parties outside the app's Tor/SOCKS transport, so any feature requiring OS location lookup structurally defeats the anonymity layer and must be removed entirely.
ideas: Android's NETWORK_PROVIDER sends Wi-Fi/cell scans to Google, bypassing any app-level proxy or Tor circuit.
Assisted GPS (SUPL) similarly phones home on cold fixes, outside app control.
Client-enforced conditions (location, locks) only deter phone seizure, not client modification.
Location predicates are themselves metadata that link network activity to geography.
Any OS call that consults external services can leak past a hardened transport layer.
Retired envelope identifiers must never be reused to avoid legacy-client misinterpretation.
items.rating_reason: Firsthand, technically precise postmortem explaining why a location-lock feature was architecturally incompatible with the app's anonymity goals. The article names specific Android APIs (GPS_PROVIDER, NETWORK_PROVIDER, SUPL), explains how Google Play Services' network provider attributes requests to a third party bypassing Tor/SOCKS, and articulates a generalizable principle: any OS-mediated call that 'looks outward' defeats transport-layer anonymity. The references to EncroChat and Ricochet failures and the concrete remediation (permission removal, envelope version retirement) add credibility.

OAuth2 bearer tokens passed as URL query parameters in SignalR long-poll requests get written to nginx access logs in plaintext
Inconsistent escaping in ufn_GetFullTextQueryString routes single-quote inputs through a path without apostrophe escaping

items.title: Guest-to-host heap overflow via integer overflow in VMXNET3 TSO segmentation (CVE-2026-59346)
items.summary: A guest-to-host heap overflow in VMware VMXNET3 TSO code bypasses CVE-2025-41236 because the prior fix validated descriptor fields individually but never validated their product, allowing a 32-bit imul truncation to produce a tiny allocation that the segmentation loop then writes far past.
ideas: Bounding multiplicands individually does not bound their product, so any product-based allocation needs its own check
32-bit imul truncation yields a heap overflow with attacker-controlled content via packet headers
IPv6 Destination Options padding provides fully guest-specified bytes that land on glibc chunk metadata
Silent glibc heap corruption enables tcache poisoning or FSOP for host code execution
VMware Workstation/Fusion 26H1u1 (VMSA-2026-0007) fixes by using 64-bit arithmetic or validating the product
VMXNET3 guest TX ring + doorbell at BAR0+0x600 is the reachable attack surface from any admin guest
items.rating_reason: Exceptional vulnerability research with original evidence including specific disassembly from the affected binary, a fully worked numerical example (688,297 × 6,240 wrapping to 5,984), and exact byte offsets for heap metadata corruption. The conceptual analysis of why CVE-2025-41236's individual-field bounds checks failed to bound their product is a non-obvious, broadly applicable lesson. The exploitation chain through IPv6 Destination Options padding to corrupt glibc heap metadata is presented with high specificity and minimal noise.

items.title: Building Alpine Linux Disk Images Without a VM
items.summary: A chroot-based, no-VM Alpine image builder that exposes non-obvious pitfalls in losetup, XFS/ext4/Btrfs mount-option remounting, GRUB removable-path installation, and Btrfs compression heuristics, with concrete fixes for each.
ideas: losetup -P returns before udev creates /dev/loopNp* nodes; escalate via udevadm settle, partx -a, then mknod
XFS logbsize is fixed at initial mount and silently downgraded on remount, so it must go in rootflags=
Btrfs compress=zstd skips ELF binaries by heuristic; use compress-force at build time
Place /boot on the ESP so GRUB only ever reads FAT, decoupling it from root FS feature changes
Use grub-install --removable --no-nvram for cloud images whose NVRAM cannot be written at build time
Pin Alpine to concrete branch (v3.24), not latest-stable, so runtime apk upgrades do not jump releases
Alpine's setup-disk assumes a booted live system and cannot be reused for image building
ext4 block size cannot exceed kernel page size (4 KiB); align via stride/stripe_width, not -b
items.rating_reason: Exceptional hands-on systems engineering write-up. The article documents real debugging incidents with full mechanism explanations: the losetup/udev partition-node race, XFS logbsize being silently downgraded because it's fixed at initial mount, the Btrfs compress heuristic that skips ELF binaries, and the rootflags= kernel cmdline trick to preserve mount options. It provides a reproducible, configurable pipeline (mkalpine.sh) with thoughtful knobs, security defaults, and concrete mkfs/mount tuning per filesystem. Highly relevant to Linux/sysadmin/infrastructure readers and dense with non-obvious, verifiable findings.

items.title: DOOM in the kernel, or fibers in eBPF
items.summary: Compiling arbitrary C to verifier-acceptable eBPF requires reshaping pointer provenance and loops so the verifier's symbolic state survives LLVM optimization, enabling DOOM, Lua, Python, SQLite, and llama2.c to run unmodified inside the stock Linux BPF JIT.
ideas: eBPF verifier tracks pointer biography that LLVM optimization can erase
Pointer laundering via map indirection bypasses scalar-pointer subtraction ban
Verifier is sometimes faster with imprecise loop initial values
Empty inline asm preserves data dependency the verifier recognizes
Canonicalizing loops to one iterator replaces knotty PHI nodes
A regions-fibers-software-stack VM emerges inside eBPF
Lua and CPython inspect XDP packets via the same Capsule compiler
BPF globals become map values, not process memory, with ELF relocations
items.rating_reason: Original, deeply technical first-hand engineering report on compiling arbitrary C/C++/Rust programs to verifier-acceptable eBPF, demonstrated by running unmodified DOOM in the Linux kernel BPF JIT. Dense with non-obvious verifier mechanics (pointer laundering via map indirection, canonicalizing loops into a single iterator, the paradox that the verifier is faster with less precise state, how LLVM's -O2 destroys verifier proofs), concrete LLVM/verifier code examples, a reproducible artifact (`nix run github:ayles/bpf-capsule#doom`), and broader applicability to Lua, QuickJS, SQLite, llama2.c, and CPython in BPF. Score docked slightly because the article is truncated mid-sentence and we do not see the final architecture, benchmarks, or conclusions.

items.title: FIPS 140-2 vs 140-3: what actually changed
items.summary: FIPS 140-3 changed the vocabulary, paperwork, and self-test timing rather than module security properties; deferred algorithm self-tests and the largely-untested non-invasive security area are the substantive technical shifts.
ideas: FIPS 140-3 defers algorithm self-tests to first use rather than at power-up, changing failure modes vs 140-2.
766 of 778 active FIPS 140-3 certificates list non-invasive security as not applicable.
60 of 75 FIPS 140-2 certificates issued since January 2024 are software, mostly OpenSSL rebrands.
114 vendors hold active 140-2 certs but have never held a 140-3 certificate, including major HSM vendors.
2019 YubiKey RNG flaw stemmed from predictable bits left by mandatory power-up self-tests that 140-3 defers.
Interim validation scheme let RHEL 9's FIPS module sunset 11 days before the broader 140-2 historical transition.
The CMVP issued 394 FIPS 140-3 certificates in the first 36 weeks of 2026 vs only 6 in 2022.
items.rating_reason: Exceptional firsthand analysis from someone running a nightly CMVP certificate tracker, with original data (5,506 certs, 766/778 listing non-invasive security as N/A, 114 vendors lacking any 140-3 cert, queue issuance curves) and concrete code references (Go's fips140/aes/cast.go). The deferred self-test analysis tied to the 2019 YubiKey RNG flaw and the rebranding pattern (60/75 recent 140-2 certs being software, often OpenSSL) deliver non-obvious practitioner insight. The central finding—that 140-3 is mostly an alignment/vocabulary exercise and the date moved more than the security properties—is well-supported and genuinely useful for procurement, compliance, and module-integration work.

Full domain relevance bonus applied for AI/ML infrastructure tooling.

items.title: https://github.com/mein-0/forti-research

ideas: FortiClient's fortimon3_74.sys exposes unauthenticated minifilter port enabling PPL bypass
Eight-byte message with magic 0x6C6C696B and PID terminates any process from kernel
Missing caller and target validation enables trivial exploitation by local admins
PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS instead of PROCESS_TERMINATE violates least privilege principle
Missing OBJ_KERNEL_HANDLE flag leaks kernel handles to usermode briefly
Signed vulnerable drivers create BYOVD attack vectors even after patching
PPL-protected processes like lsass.exe remain vulnerable via kernel driver abuse
PoC terminates Defender or any process by name with simple command-line argument
Responsible disclosure to Fortinet PSIRT resulted in duplicate finding
Linux/macOS naively trust kernel-mode handles without proper user/kernel separation
items.rating_reason: Genuine, well-documented vulnerability disclosure with high technical density. Provides specific exploit details (8-byte message structure with magic 0x6C6C696B), identifies multiple root causes, includes a working PoC and video demo, and documents responsible disclosure. JIT-for-weights with learned expert pinning and lookahead prefetch
Single C-file engine with zero runtime dependencies
Multi-backend support: CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, plus CPU
Dual-SSD weighted striping for decode bandwidth aggregation
Cluster coordinator for disk-backed expert workers over TCP
Token-exact forward validation and quality-bounded quantization
Live expert visualization as a 'brain' cortex of routing heat

items.summary: An authenticated marketing email from Carnival Cruise Line was routing recipients to malware through a lapsed promotional domain that had been wired into a cloaked redirection network, demonstrating how domain hygiene failures create authentic-looking attack vectors that bypass both email authentication and security scanners.
ideas: Authenticated emails (SPF/DKIM/DMARC passing) can still deliver malware via lapsed promotional domains
Cloaking redirects scanners to clean pages while real browsers reach malware payloads
PseudoJack uses .appinstaller manifests with forced auto-update channels for persistent access
PhantomJack packages pad to ~148MB to exceed antivirus and sandbox size scan thresholds
Browser lockers abuse Pointer Lock API, synthesized voice, and fake scrolling terminals
Per-advertiser reporting fails because monetization services replace removed advertisers quickly
Parked domain monetization chains funnel leftover traffic into malware delivery networks
Anti-analysis debugger traps build at runtime, evading static scanner detection
Malware certificates use bare GUIDs as organization names, valid for only 3 days
Domain hygiene failure: domain lapsed November 2024 while live marketing mail still linked to it
Exposure window ran from November 2024 lapse to August 2026 domain re-acquisition
Real visitors get fingerprinted and routed differently than datacenter scanners or headless browsers
urlscan.io flagged the page as one of 10,000+ similar, indicating a templated cloaking network
Microsoft disabled ms-appinstaller protocol handler in 2023 due to Storm-1113 and others abusing it
items.rating_reason: Original threat intelligence research documenting a genuine malware delivery path through authenticated Carnival Cruise Line marketing emails routed via a lapsed promotional domain. Delivers multiple novel insights: the PseudoJack variant with .appinstaller auto-update channels, cloaking behavior that fools both scanners and reputation services, ~148MB payload padding to bypass AV size thresholds, and browser locker techniques using Pointer Lock API. items.title: gabdevele@dev

ideas: sqlite_dbpage provides low-level read/write access to raw database pages
SQLite header has immutable bytes at offsets 24-27, 92-95, and 96-99
Relocate ELF Program Header Table to binary's end to avoid header corruption
Python .so shared objects take precedence over .py files during module resolution
Gunicorn's 30-second timeout can crash workers and force module reload
Recursive zeroblob queries exhaust memory to crash managed processes
PRAGMA page_size=65536 enables writing entire binary in single UPDATE statement
SQLite ATTACH DATABASE requires non-existent or valid existing database file

Use LIEF library's relocate_phdr_table to move ELF PHDR safely
Cythonize Python modules into .so files for stronger module hijacking
Puma's preload_app prevents direct shadowing but imports nio4r on restart
items.rating_reason: Exceptional original security research presenting a novel RCE technique via SQLite's sqlite_dbpage virtual table. The post delivers multiple genuinely novel insights: precise identification of immutable SQLite header bytes, ELF Program Header Table relocation workaround, cross-language applicability (Python and Ruby), and practical crash-to-restart trigger methods. Code examples are concrete and reproducible, and the research builds credibly on prior work with clear attribution. The sandbox paradoxically causes permission prompts to disappear because Seatbelt handles sandboxing

The git ls-files refresh command was left unhardened, bypassing core.fsmonitor protection
Claude's .git folder write protection only covers the root directory, not nested subdirectories
Bash tool retains last-used directory, letting attackers redirect harness git calls elsewhere
Skill auto-loading on file reads can trigger automatic file index refreshes for exploitation
Anthropic fully fixed the exploit chain in Claude Code 2.1.247 after responsible disclosure
VM-based agent isolation with credential placeholders and proxy-based network control is a robust defense

The post delivers 6+ distinct value instances including the novel sandbox escape finding, precise technical breakdown of four defense bypasses (core.fsmonitor exploitation, unhardened git ls-files, nested .git folder gap, and skill auto-loading abuse), a responsible disclosure timeline, and a sound architectural recommendation (VM isolation with credential placeholders). The final section promoting the authors' product 'Accomplish' introduces mild hidden promotion but also provides genuinely useful architectural guidance, warranting a small deduction rather than a major one.

items.title: Hey Siri, welcome to my Minecraft server
items.summary: A full reverse-engineering path from a Minecraft chat command to a working Linux Siri client, covering ACE protocol framing, plist command layout, FairPlay SAP V1 authentication, and ARM64e emulation in Unicorn.
ideas: ACE is a literal HTTP/2 method name, not a framework
AA CC EE 02 is three fixed bytes plus a compression-type argument
Modern Siri uses a flat ACE object layout, not the nested legacy shape
SAP V1 FairPlay does not require real Mac hardware secrets
PAC instructions can be stripped for ARM64e emulation under Unicorn
Dyld chained fixups must be walked and rebased before emulation
Older Absinthe NAC emulator (strategy 2) is rejected by current Siri
Synchronization must complete before text requests flow successfully
Bidirectional HTTP/2 stream stays open the whole Siri session
Platform strings aren't bound to the FairPlay SAP output
items.rating_reason: Original, deeply technical reverse-engineering writeup of Apple's current ACE Siri protocol, including HTTP/2 framing, plist command serialization, FairPlay SAP V1 authentication, ARM64e PAC bypass, and dyld chained fixup rebase for Unicorn emulation on Linux. Includes source snippets, honest discussion of dead ends (the older NAC emulator), reproducible concrete steps, build-specific addresses, and explicit caveats about what was and wasn't accomplished. The SAP V1 finding that it doesn't actually read real Mac hardware secrets (only kern.hv_vmm_present) is a non-obvious, security-relevant observation.

items.title: Rebuilding a Lost iOS Game: From Screenshots to Reverse Engineering to AI
items.summary: Recovering a delisted encrypted iOS game via jailbreak and FairPlay decryption, then reverse-engineering its exact piece distribution and scoring rules to benchmark AI agents where expectimax outperformed greedy, learned, neural, and rollout baselines.
ideas: Delisted but previously purchased iOS apps can still be downloaded via ipatool-py and decrypted on a jailbroken device
Block Crush Blitz hex mode uses 22 uniformly distributed pieces (one dot + 21 four-cell shapes)
Score formula: distinct cells removed + lineCount × (10 + 5 × (lineCount − 1))
Expectimax averaged 3,721 vs rollout 3,257 over 20 seeded games; lookahead beat learning
A small neural evaluator (2,532) lost to a handwritten one (5,074) on the same seeds
items.rating_reason: Substantive firsthand engineering across multiple technical domains: iOS app recovery (ipatool-py, FairPlay cryptid=1, palera1n jailbreak via DFU, ipadecrypt via iproxy/libusbmuxd), concrete reverse-engineering findings with Binary Ninja (22-piece catalog with uniform 1/22 selection, exact scoring formula with line bonuses of 10/30/60/100), and a clean agent benchmark (expectimax averaging 3,721.55 vs rollout 3,256.90 vs greedy 1,055.30 vs random 49.75 over 20 seeded games). The observation that lookahead dominates learning, and that a small neural net (2,532) actually underperformed a handwritten evaluator (5,074) on the same seeds, is a useful practical finding. Limits: some personal narrative padding and the benchmark scope is modest.

items.title: Inspect: Read the Bits
items.summary: A pocket tool plus tutorial that teaches subtle C integer-promotion, signed/unsigned conversion, IEEE 754, and byte-order semantics through interactive selection of numbers, dumps, and expressions.
ideas: 'Unsigned always wins' ignores width: -1L < 0U is true because long holds every unsigned int.
Integer literal type is decided before negation: 2147483648 is long, making -2147483648 long.
COERCE_FLOAT reinterprets bits; (float) cast converts value - same 0x3f800000 yields different results.
uint8_t promotes to int before ~, so ~(uint8_t)0 yields -1, not 255.
Hex dumps record byte order; debugger words like 0x41424344 are already host-order numbers.
Decimal literals round directly to float32, preserving precision vs float64-then-narrow.
Uppercase NAN/INFINITY are float32; lowercase are float64, matching C macros.
IDA _BYTE/_WORD/_DWORD/_QWORD casts interpret a constant as that many little-endian bytes.
items.rating_reason: Dense, well-illustrated documentation for a browser-based binary inspector that doubles as a tutorial on non-obvious C semantics and binary representation. The article is not promotional fluff: it explicitly teaches counter-intuitive points such as width defeating the 'unsigned always wins' rule (-1L < 0U is true), integer-promotion effects on casts and ~, the cast-vs-COERCE distinction for bit reinterpretation, and how different dump formats (xxd, hexdump, GDB, pwndbg) carry byte-order information. It is highly relevant to reverse engineering, vulnerability research, and low-level programming, with minimal noise and concrete reproducible examples throughout.
items.image_alt: Entropic — Research Philes: vulnerability research, reverse engineering, and exploitation notes.

items.title: From Raw Memory to Structured Web Applications
items.summary: A maintainer's deep dive into giving Ruby I/O buffers explicit ownership, formalizing scheduler hooks, bounding untrusted content parsing, and rebuilding Utopia around protocol objects instead of Rack hashes.
ideas: IO::Buffer slices now retain their root buffer, so freeing the root invalidates every view
Buffer locks are reference counted to support overlapping users safely
Scheduler hooks perform one transfer; higher-level IO decides waiting/retry
Protocol parsers enforce explicit size, pair-count, and nesting-depth limits
Protocol::URL::Path preserves encoded slashes to avoid filesystem traversal
Utopia 3 replaces Rack with Utopia::Application on Protocol::HTTP middleware
Accept#preferred_media_ranges preserves source order for equal q-values
items.rating_reason: Dense, original engineering journal from a maintainer deeply embedded in Ruby's I/O, async, and web stack. Contains concrete code, explicit ownership/lifetime models for IO::Buffer, security-aware bounded parsing (DoS limits, encoded slash vs filesystem separator), and a substantial architecture shift (Utopia 3 replacing Rack with Protocol::HTTP middleware). Content is truncated near the end, but the delivered material is high in substance, mechanisms, and reproducible detail with no hype or padding.

items.title: A faster way to calculate the Time of Day
items.summary: By reordering the H/M/S decomposition into two parallel dependency chains of length 4 and applying fixed-point and base-64 modulus-padding tricks, daily timestamp-to-time-of-day conversion can be reduced to roughly 5 CPU cycles of latency versus ~8–16 in mainstream date libraries.
ideas: Compute tmin and hour first in parallel, then derive minute/second independently to break chains.
Use mul-shift fixed-point division (e.g., *71582789>>32 for /60) when input is bounded to ~626 hours.
Pad-mod trick: x mod 60 equals (x + 4*(x/60)) mod 64, turning costly divmod into a mask.
LEA/LSL#2 instructions compute time + 4*tmin in a single cycle on x86 and ARM.
Total achievable latency is ~5 cycles, beating Lemire/Neri's ~8-cycle prior art.
JIT/compilers often fail to recognize these algebraic rearrangements automatically.
items.rating_reason: Exceptional systems-level performance engineering article presenting multiple novel algorithms for converting seconds-of-day to H/M/S with explicit cycle-latency tables, derivation of magic constants, real benchmarks on AMD Ryzen 9 and Apple M4 Pro, and comparison against implementations in the Linux kernel, glibc, Go, CPython, OpenJDK, V8, Boost, musl, and .NET. The 'parallel decomposition' (computing hour and tmin independently, then deriving minute and second in a second parallel phase) and the base-64 modulus-padding trick (x mod 60 = (x + 4*floor(x/60)) mod 64) appear to be original contributions with no prior precedent in date libraries. Limitations (range restrictions, throughput vs latency tradeoffs) are honestly disclosed. Article is slightly truncated at the end.

items.title: Predicting the Go Linker
items.summary: Because the Go linker derives most of the binary from the function list by deterministic rules, a patcher that models the linker can predict nearly every byte after a small edit and ship only the delta plus a correction, yielding 30x smaller patches than bsdiff on Go release binaries.
ideas: Go binaries are ~half tables derived from the function list, making them highly predictable from edits.
One 200-byte source edit amplified to 14% of bytes changed because addresses and table offsets shift.
Predicted then corrected beats chunk-dedup and slide-finding for linker-derived formats.
Presage encodes a function-list diff as the plan and falls back to a generic ELF module when unsupported.
DWARF is a second amplifier addressable by unwrapping compression and predicting structure layer by layer.
Linker-version coupling (Go 1.27 moved type descriptors, changed debug compressor) requires per-version models.
Release hashes plus BLAKE3 plus a small correction bytes lets the decoder verify predictions safely.
presage is open source at wjordan/presage and supports Go 1.26 and 1.27 today.
items.rating_reason: Original technical work describing presage, a binary patcher that models Go's linker to predict most of a new binary from the old one plus a small edit. Provides concrete benchmarks (1.1 KB vs 150 KB bsdiff for a one-line change; 80 KB vs 2.7 MB for a Prometheus release), detailed byte-level mechanism (192-byte handler growth propagating as 34-byte table shifts, recursing into offsets throughout .gopclntab, .rodata, ELF, DWARF, FIPS HMAC), and honest discussion of linker-version coupling. Dense, low-noise, and reproducibly grounded with comparisons against xdelta3, bsdiff, Zucchini, and rsync on real artifacts. The only minor limits are the narrow applicability surface (Go binaries today, Chrome via a generic ELF module) and that it is a single-author tool write-up rather than peer-reviewed measurement.

items.title: PHP 8.6 Gives Streams Real Errors, and You Can Finally Stop Parsing Warning Strings
items.summary: PHP 8.6 replaces fragile warning-string parsing on stream failures with typed StreamError objects, an error_mode context option (Error/Exception/Silent), and stream_last_errors(), enabling reliable programmatic error handling.
ideas: Use StreamErrorMode::Exception with try/catch on StreamException for application code paths.
Compare StreamErrorCode enum cases instead of substring matching on error messages.
One stream call can produce multiple errors, so iterate the array from stream_last_errors().
stream_select, stream_copy_to_stream, stream_socket_pair, and stream_is_local gained optional context parameters.
Cannot set error_mode on the default context; you must pass an explicit context you created.
Exception mode only throws for terminating errors, not warnings like buffer truncation.
PHP 8.6 hard freeze is September 24, 2026; GA targeted November 19, 2026.
Implementation coverage is still being filled in; unconverted wrappers still emit old-style errors.
items.rating_reason: Substantive, well-sourced walkthrough of the PHP 8.6 stream error handling RFC with concrete code examples, the new API surface (StreamErrorMode, StreamError, stream_last_errors()), 70+ StreamErrorCode cases, design rationale (arrays over linked lists), and the deliberate restriction against configuring the default context. Includes versioned timeline and honest caveats about incomplete implementation coverage. Falls short of exceptional because it is primarily explanatory documentation of a single RFC rather than original investigation or measurement.

items.title: Stop Asking Claude to Run Pint: Enforce Your PHP Toolchain With Hooks
items.summary: A complete, well-tested configuration for enforcing PHP quality (Pint, PHPStan, Pest) via Claude Code hooks, with several non-obvious findings about exit codes, prompt-injection-safe framing, and loop prevention.
ideas: Exit code 2 is the blocking exit for Claude Code hooks; exit 1 only logs a notice.
Stderr from a hook that exits 0 is invisible to the model.
Phrase additionalContext as factual statements to avoid prompt-injection defenses.
Use a guard file pattern to let Stop hooks fire once before standing down.
Analyse single files, not the whole project, to keep hook latency under a second.
Broken hooks (exit 127) fail silently—always verify the first run.
The 'if' matcher holds exactly one rule and no AND/OR operators.
items.rating_reason: This is a densely practical, technically substantive article with complete, copy-paste-ready code for configuring Claude Code hooks. It surfaces multiple non-obvious findings: exit code 2 (not 1) is the blocking code, stderr from exit 0 is invisible to the model, additionalContext phrasing matters for prompt-injection defenses, and the Stop hook needs a guard file to prevent infinite loops. Every claim is grounded in either code or a specific mechanism, with no padding or hype.

items.summary: A substantial tour of the git-pkgs ecosystem of Go supply-chain tools, with original performance numbers, security-focused design rationales, and a modular architecture that deliberately isolates heavy dependencies like TUF, Fulcio, and Rekor.

items.title: The Index Structures of Fast C++ Hash Maps
items.summary: An expert source-code survey of 18 hash map implementations reveals that erase strategy (tombstones vs. overflow bits vs. counters vs. backward shift vs. chained metadata) is the central design decision, and that single-size benchmarks are systematically misleading because performance swings by 1.25x–1.83x between doublings.
ideas: Erase strategies: tombstones, overflow bits, counters, backward shift, or chained metadata
Fingerprint bits must come from opposite end of hash to avoid correlation with home
Hash map performance forms a sawtooth between doublings, often 1.25x–1.83x wide
Dependent loads dominate lookup cost for large tables, not branch mispredictions
Most design differences collapse to roughly two assembly instructions on probe loops
A single-size benchmark can reverse the sign of a comparison between two maps
items.rating_reason: Original, source-driven analysis of 18 C++ hash map index structures with a unifying taxonomy (the 'five questions'), original benchmarks on one machine with a transparent octave-averaging methodology, and assembly-level analysis showing performance differences collapse to roughly two instructions. Author discloses his own design (unordered_dense) but the prior 95% of the work analyzes other libraries from source, including non-obvious bugs (ixhtab). Highly non-obvious content: why robin hood has the worst sawtooth, why fingerprint bits must come from the opposite end of the hash, and how a one-size sample can reverse the sign of a comparison.

items.title: Campfire, Cached
items.summary: A real Rails app benchmarked on three runtimes reveals that a fragment cache moved in-process, a transitive `after_touch` fix, and an SQLite synchronous-mode default are each worth an order of magnitude or more — and that the headline compiler speedup is mostly the GVL, not codegen.
ideas: belongs_to touch: true silently no-ops when subclasses override Base#touch; fix is firing after_touch
Cache keys must namespace page renders vs WebSocket broadcasts because broadcast omits CSRF
Three benchmark lanes ran different SQLite synchronous settings because the binary linked its own SQLite
Mark phase scales with parked green-thread stack depth, not worker count directly
Roundhouse lowering gives ~4.7x; Spinel compiler adds ~2.5x; factors multiply on top of GVL difference
GC spends 49% of wall time in collector on the room page; mark is the dominant phase
Remembered-set clear walking the whole old heap on every non-full GC cost up to 67% under threads
The 2.8x headline speedup is almost entirely 8 CRuby processes vs 6 workers in one binary
Per-core binary vs CRuby is close (1.24x room, 0.98x messages) — codegen parity, not a leap
Action Cable registry is per-process, so multi-process CRuby deployment silently loses broadcasts
items.rating_reason: Exceptionally substantive engineering write-up with original measurements, multiple non-obvious discoveries (silent no-op on `touch: true` callbacks, three lanes inadvertently running different SQLite durability settings, GC mark phase tracking parked-fiber stack depth rather than worker count), and rigorous separation of compiler contribution from lowering contribution. The author is unusually honest about limitations and what the data cannot support, including per-core caveats and the deployability gap of the CRuby lane. Direct practical implications for anyone working on Ruby/Rails performance, runtime engineering, or benchmark methodology.

items.title: Concise Introduction to Gated DeltaNets
items.summary: Gated DeltaNets combine decay gating with a delta-rule update on a fixed-size state to give linear attention that forgets gracefully and can overwrite prior values, interpretable as online gradient descent on a regression objective.
ideas: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a D_v × D_k state, yielding O(1) updates and constant memory.
Naive linear accumulation causes unbounded growth and blind writes; decay gates fix forgetting.
The delta rule update equals a per-token gradient step on a least-squares recall loss.
For unit-norm keys, I - βkk^T scales the key direction by 1-β, giving an erase-then-write reading.
β_t acts as a learned per-token learning rate controlling old-vs-new value interpolation.
items.rating_reason: A focused, mathematically rigorous walkthrough of Gated DeltaNets that derives the mechanism step-by-step from softmax attention to linear attention to delta-rule updates. It offers two non-obvious interpretive frames — test-time regression (the update is a gradient step on a least-squares recall loss) and the erase-then-write view (with a clean proof that I - βkk^T scales the k direction by 1-β). Limitations: it is a synthesis of existing papers rather than new research, and includes no empirical comparisons or implementation guidance.

Interface merging cannot replace signatures; Omit defeats loose-signature fallthrough.
Virtual TS files without imports/exports become ambient scripts sharing global scope; export {} fixes it.
Bun.child_process.fork spawns Bun, masking Node TypeScript strip-mode bugs in test runs.
Fixture corpus with atText offset anchors is the spec; agents work unsupervised against shared fixtures.
Emit template constructs as real control flow so tsc infers types from loops and branches.

items.title: How Miri found a data race in a lock-free ring buffer that the compiler had no way to see

ideas: Deref/DerefMut through generic trait bounds creates wide references that retag full allocations
Stacked Borrows treats any reference (re)creation as a real read or write over its range
Miri needs -Zmiri-preemption-rate=0.1 to surface races the interpreter would otherwise miss
Concurrency tests for Miri must be small enough to interpret but force producer/consumer overlap
SAFETY comments must audit reference width, not only the slots the index expression touches
cargo miri test passing does not imply absence of UB in multi-threaded code
items.rating_reason: Exceptional technical depth on a subtle Rust aliasing bug. The article meticulously explains how automatic Deref/DerefMut insertion through a generic trait bound silently widens a reference to the entire allocation, triggering a retag that violates Stacked Borrows even when the SPSC protocol's slot-level invariants hold. ideas: Go's os.Open on Linux issues fcntl+epoll_ctl for every regular file because netpoll refuses; switching to syscall.Open cuts syscalls ~15x
A pipeline bottleneck (one stat-file goroutine, eight walkers) caused 100% full potentialFilesQueue and 134k futex calls

items.title: Half Past Fetch
items.summary: fetch() resolves when headers arrive, not when the body finishes, so ignoring response.body silently burns HTTP/1.1 connections in Node from 16KB upward and clones form tees that retain every chunk until the unused branch is drained or cancelled.
ideas: fetch() resolves when response headers arrive, body is still streaming
Unread bodies ≥16KB kill Node HTTP/1.1 keep-alive; Chrome tolerates ~512KB
response.body.cancel() does NOT return the socket to the pool
clone() is a tee over the live stream, not a memory copy
Abandoned clone branch retains full payload (~55MB for 60MB response)
Awaiting cancel() on one tee branch deadlocks until the other finishes
Reading any chunk or arrayBuffer makes later clone() throw TypeError
bodyUsed is per-Response, not shared between cloned branches
items.rating_reason: Exceptional technical investigation that combines spec-level analysis with reproducible experiments and hard numbers. The article demonstrates (with measured evidence across Node and Chrome) that fetch() resolves on headers, not body; quantifies the connection-pool cost of ignoring bodies (Node ≥16KB, Chrome ≥512KB); shows clone() is a tee that doubles memory (~55MB for a 60MB response); and reveals the deadlock when awaiting cancel() on one branch before reading the other. Content is truncated at the abort section, which is a real limitation, but the delivered substance is original, expert-level, and immediately actionable for production web/server code.

ideas: Token-2022 confidential transfer fee logic had a forgeable OR-proof fixable by appending one scalar to the Fiat-Shamir transcript.
Native confidential transfers require three transactions because the three ZK proofs exceed Solana's per-transaction size limit.
Transfer amounts are capped at 48 bits because ElGamal decryption time grows with the value.
Helius Rings currently requires wallet to send plaintext recipient, asset, amount, and nullifier keys to Helius for proving.
Confidential transfer extension must be opted into at mint creation; legacy SPL tokens cannot gain it.
Auditor key lets a designated ElGamal pubkey decrypt but never spend transfers on a regulated mint.

items.rating_reason: A firsthand incident postmortem with unusual forensic depth: the author reconstructs the full attack chain of CVE-2026-60004, documents the attackers' clever exfiltration channel (git hooks writing command output as commits read back via the web UI), recovers an unlinked miner binary from /proc/PID/exe, and shares concrete IoCs including hashes, C2 endpoints, and persistence paths. Several hard-won, non-obvious lessons elevate it beyond a routine writeup: persistence surviving in a bind-mounted data volume where container recreation would reinfected, master-key rotation silently breaking LDAP authentication with 500 errors, and the installer's persistence-mechanism fallback sequence. Relevance to the reader's security, Linux, and infrastructure interests is direct, evidence is original, and the only limitations are the small scale of the incident and conventional root causes (EOL pinning, open registration).

items.title: https://blog.securelayer7.net/cve-2026-10520-ivanti-sentry-os-command-injection/
items.summary: Ivanti Sentry's pre-auth root RCE exists because a deliberately designed command-execution feature in its configuration API relied on network isolation instead of application-layer authentication, leaving any caller reaching port 8443 able to execute unsanitized commands and read their output.
ideas: Unauthenticated POST to the MICS handleMessage endpoint yields root-level command execution on Ivanti Sentry
'execute' is a designed allowlist verb in the config API; the flaw is unguarded reachability, not a smuggled command
StringTokenizer round-trip preserves multi-word commands via single spaces but forbids tab or newline separation

Network-layer isolation assumptions replaced real authentication once MICS API was consolidated onto shared port 8443
Command stdout returns inline in the JSON response body, making the injection non-blind with no out-of-band callback needed
validateXPath checks only the destination path, never the payload, so commandexec arguments reach the shell unsanitized
Reflection-based native dispatch resolves methods by string name, converting a configuration API into a command executor
HTTP 400/500 confirms a vulnerable reachable endpoint; 302 indicates patched; 404 means MICS service is not running
The reqandres XML element is deliberately overloaded to carry command input inbound and command stdout outbound
items.rating_reason: This is dense, expert-level vulnerability research containing roughly ten distinct value instances: a fully traced root-cause chain across four decompiled Java classes (controller, tokenizer, validator, reflection dispatcher), a working PoC with the exact request format, practical patch-verification observables (400/500 vs 302 vs 404), and genuinely novel analysis such as the StringTokenizer whitespace round-trip that makes multi-word commands survive to the sink, and the observation that 'execute' is a designed allowlist verb rather than a smuggled input. The content properly attributes watchTowr, Rapid7, and CrowdSec while adding original decomposition beyond their writeups, avoiding any rehash penalty. Strong thematic alignment with CyberSecurity and enterprise infrastructure defense; the only mild limitation is that the core discovery is derivative of already-published research rather than original.

ldd on an hour-old binary and 'Nothing to be done' made measurement lie

items.title: The line that makes every attribute access 50% slower
items.summary: Since CPython 3.11 attribute access uses a fixed-offset inline values array, and any read of __dict__ (including via vars() or copy.copy()) permanently materializes a real dict that makes every subsequent attribute access about 50% slower — so __slots__ is the real protective fix.
ideas: Reading __dict__ once permanently deoptimizes CPython attribute access to a real dict
Since 3.11, LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE reads a fixed byte offset, not a hash table
LOAD_ATTR_WITH_HINT refuses split-table dicts, leaving materialized objects unspecialized
__slots__ doesn't speed up reads; it prevents materialization by removing __dict__
Free-threaded builds add acquire loads, try-incref, and per-object mutex on stores
Hoisted locals beat attribute access by 1.33x, but the dict explanation is obsolete
items.rating_reason: Original pyperf benchmarks with error bounds, adaptive-bytecode disassembly, and CPython source excerpts show that the classic attribute-hoisting explanation has been wrong since 3.11, and that a single __dict__ read (directly or via vars()/copy.copy()) permanently demotes an object to unspecialized dict access roughly 50% slower. The investigation is rigorous: control benchmarks isolate the attribute cost, the split-table rejection explains why no hint specialization applies, __slots__ assumptions are tested and corrected, and free-threaded builds are analyzed down to atomic loads and per-object mutexes. Practical applicability is honestly bounded to hot inner loops, but the invisible materialization footgun is genuinely actionable and non-obvious. This is expert firsthand runtime-internals work with exceptional evidence quality and near-zero noise.

items.title: Worktrees in Production: Blue-Green Deploys from One Clone
items.summary: Blue-green deploys using a bare repo plus two detached worktrees and an `ln -sfn` symlink flip are cheap and atomic, but require attention to several non-obvious gotchas around hook exit codes, worktree pruning, and the mv/cp symlink-to-directory follow behavior.
ideas: `ln -sfn` on the symlink replaces it atomically; `mv` of a temp symlink follows an existing live link into its target directory.
`post-merge` hook failures do not propagate back to `git pull`'s exit code; orchestrators must inspect side effects.
Two `git worktree` checkouts share one object database, so blue/green cost only working-tree disk, not full history.
Detached HEAD is required because git refuses to check the same branch into two worktrees simultaneously.
`rm -rf` of a worktree dir leaves a `prunable` entry that blocks `git worktree add` at the same path until `prune` runs.
`-T`/`--no-target-directory` is GNU-only; BSD `mv` (macOS) has no equivalent opt-out for symlink-to-dir follow.
items.rating_reason: Substantive, reproducible technical writing on a real production pattern with multiple non-obvious findings. The article demonstrates the mv/cp directory-following symlink bug with concrete output, explains why detached HEAD is required for worktree deploy targets, surfaces the post-merge hook's failure-not-propagating behavior, and documents the prunable worktree state left by `rm -rf`. Hooks are runnable and well-commented, and trade-offs are explicit. Minor caveats: future-dated post (Sep 2026) and one line of author bio padding, but core content is excellent.

items.title: The Case of the Interrupt That Arrived Too Soon: A Ruby Mystery

Stream partial results for progressive response, improving time‑to‑first‑useful.
Apply concurrency budgets to limit parallel work and protect shared resources.
Use hedged requests to mitigate straggler impact by sending duplicate calls.

Levels 6-7 (cross-engine, cross-vendor) are coordination problems: no contract artefact exists.
Same engineer filed the divergence as a bug but implemented the fix as a feature, correctly.

items.title: Show HN: Ringdl2 – A lightweight Linux downloader in Rust using io_uring
items.summary: Ringdl2 achieves dramatically lower memory and CPU overhead by using io_uring, O_DIRECT, and a pinned memory pool to bypass traditional buffering during HTTPS downloads.
ideas: Unified io_uring interface merges network reads and disk writes in a single ring buffer.
Pinned memory pool registered with kernel minimizes page cache inflation.
O_DIRECT bypasses page cache, writing directly to storage device.
In-place TLS decryption and compaction satisfy O_DIRECT alignment constraints.
Write pool provides natural backpressure, throttling server via TCP flow control.
Benchmarks show 99.5% less page cache growth and 55% lower user CPU usage.
Minor page faults drop 82% while major faults reduce by 90%.
Architecture requires Linux 5.1+ and modern filesystems like ext4, XFS, Btrfs.
Memory trade‑off: higher resident set (~260 MB) vs minimal page cache usage.
Roadmap aims to extend features for a complete aria2c alternative.
items.rating_reason: The piece delivers multiple novel architectural insights (e.g., unified io_uring I/O, pinned memory pool, in-place TLS decryption) and backs them with rigorous benchmark data showing dramatic reductions in page cache usage and CPU time. It also discusses important trade-offs and a clear roadmap, aligning strongly with technology and systems themes without any padding or clickbait.
