items.title: Can an AI agent serve at a Foreign Office?
items.summary: A 10-day pilot of an LLM agent acting as a diplomatic desk officer surfaced specific failure modes—incoherence about its own actions, inability to treat silence as a tool, missing clarifications in ambiguous instructions—that demand-side workflow evaluation catches but output-only evals miss.

Output-quality evals miss most agent failures; only monitoring behavior against task workflows surfaces them

Agents often proceed on first-parse interpretation of ambiguous instructions rather than asking to clarify
Agents will propose actions outside their capability space (e.g., attending calls) without recognizing the mismatch
Demand-side evaluation frameworks grounded in practitioner workflows catch different failures than benchmark evals
Strategic ambiguity, partial information, and contested facts make diplomatic tasks a useful eval domain

items.title: prometheus: a 117GB WAL that could not truncate
items.summary: Prometheus WAL truncation only completes on successful head compaction, so an OOM during compaction creates a deadlock where the WAL grows indefinitely; deleting it requires stopping the pod via the Prometheus CR (not the StatefulSet) and avoiding the subPath mount trap.
ideas: Prometheus WAL truncation is gated on head compaction committing, so OOM during compaction creates a self-reinforcing growth loop.
Kubernetes subPath mounts can make deletes silently succeed while removing zero bytes from the underlying volume.
prometheus-operator reverts manual StatefulSet scale changes; patch the Prometheus CR's replicas field instead.
Thanos shipper's uploaded-block list proves it is safe to delete the local WAL on the PVC.
A pod memory limit set to 93% of node allocatable leaves no headroom to raise it without eviction.
items.rating_reason: A dense, first-hand SRE postmortem that documents a cascading Prometheus failure with concrete commands, outputs, and non-obvious findings: the WAL/compaction OOM deadlock, the Kubernetes subPath mount trap that would have made a delete look successful while removing nothing, and the correct lever (Prometheus CR replicas, not StatefulSet) for stopping the pod without operator-induced restart. The five-hour sample loss is honestly acknowledged, and the Thanos shipper state making the WAL deletion safe is shown directly. Very high signal-to-noise for the ~2 minute read.

items.title: When Agents Call Agents
items.summary: When agents invoke other agents via ordinary MCP tool calls, each authorization decision sees only the immediate principal and not the originating task, so shadow delegation chains can produce consequential actions (like production rollbacks) authorized by investigation-scoped requests—none of the five common approaches (token forwarding, per-agent identities, OAuth token exchange, centralized policy engines, or restricting write access) actually solves this without propagating task lineage through every hop.
ideas: Shadow delegation: tool-call chains hide the on-behalf-of relationship from enforcement points.
Every handoff in a delegation chain carries forward the original credential unchanged.
RFC 8693 token exchange creates no tight linkage between input and output tokens.
MCP Enterprise-Managed Authorization issues one token per client-server connection, so it cannot narrow as work passes between agents.
Production rollback authorization succeeds because the Deployment Agent's standing identity permits it, regardless of investigation-only intent.
Policy engines (OPA, Cedar) only enforce delegation if invocation authority is fed in as live input data.
CrewAI's Delegate work to coworker signature lacks a parameter for the authority the task confers.
Inner agents receive only tool-call arguments, not the outer agent's full conversation or reasoning context.
OWASP ASI03 attributes agent authorization failures to agents lacking governed identities of their own.
items.rating_reason: Exceptional technical depth on a non-obvious security problem: multi-agent tool-call delegation chains that current authorization frameworks cannot evaluate because the originating task context is lost at each hop. The article is densely evidenced with specific vendor behaviors (Glean, Salesforce, Snowflake, Microsoft, CrewAI), exact RFC limitations (8693, 9396), and concrete failure modes for five distinct approaches (token forwarding, standing identity, token exchange, policy engines, action restriction). The analysis is original, falsifiable, and operationally relevant to anyone deploying agentic systems. Truncation mid-sentence in section 5 prevents full evaluation of the final approach and conclusion, costing a few points.

Reviewer model choice mattered more than worker model for bugs flagged per commit
Compacting at 60% instead of 93% of the context window likely cuts near-full cache-read costs
Switching worker builds from Release to Debug cut build time by ~30%
Mechanical blockers (webhooks, disabled tests) eliminated waste that soft instructions couldn't
CI polling, sleep, and idle were the largest pure-time wastes in agent sessions
items.rating_reason: Exceptionally substantive, first-hand empirical audit of a multi-agent decompilation system. The article delivers concrete numbers throughout: tool-call time breakdowns, token/cache metrics, subagent redundancy measurements (54.7% of large-file reads duplicated), commit-rate comparisons (243.9 vs 311.1/day with/without subagents), and a cross-model build-failure and bug-detection matrix. items.title: Reading JPAK
items.summary: A reverse-engineering walkthrough showing how TOCA Race Driver 3's JPAK format was identified as an LZSS variant with a 4,096-byte space-filled ring buffer and LSB-first flag bits, derived by reading the cleartext directory, guessing a plaintext file, and tracing the first back-reference rather than brute-forcing parameters.
ideas: JPAK uses LZSS with a 4,096-byte ring buffer pre-filled with spaces (Okumura's LARC/LHarc layout)
Flag bits are consumed least-significant-first, a common reverse-engineering pitfall
Operand is a ring buffer position, not a back-distance: position = b0 | ((b1 & 0xf0) << 4)
Read the uncompressed directory first to isolate a guessable plaintext file
Trace the first back-reference to discover bit order, don't brute-force parameter tables
Demand exact uncompressed sizes on every member to validate the codec
items.rating_reason: Firsthand reverse-engineering writeup of a closed LZSS variant with strong concrete evidence: hex dumps, the specific bit-packing formula, the LSB-first flag-bit ordering, the ring-buffer-with-spaces operand interpretation, and validation across 166 files in two archives. The author is honest about a failed brute-force approach and distills a generalizable four-step methodology.
